summary.text: A singular matrix is a square matrix with no inverse, which is the same as det (A) = 0.
Its columns and rows are linearly dependent, so the map it describes is not one-to-one and the equation Ax = 0 has nonzero solutions.
Singular matrices turn up in practice, for example in regression with collinear predictors and in projections from 3D to 2D.

facts.label: Determinant test
facts.value: An n by n matrix is singular exactly when det (A) = 0

facts.label: Regression
facts.value: Collinear predictors make the normal equations matrix singular

facts.label: Graph Laplacian
facts.value: Always singular, since each row sums to zero

facts.label: Projections
facts.value: 3D to 2D projections are modeled by singular matrices

items.prompt: A square matrix has a determinant of zero. Someone tries to find another matrix that undoes it. What happens?

options.label: One always exists if you search long enough
None exists, because the matrix is not invertible
Exactly two exist, one for each side
One exists, but only for square roots

items.explain: A matrix is singular exactly when its determinant is zero, and singular means it has no inverse.

items.prompt: A graphics program squashes 3D points onto a flat screen with a matrix. Why can it not recover the original 3D positions from the result?

options.label: The screen has far too many pixels to count
The matrix has too many rows to be undone
The depth values are always negative numbers
It collapses a dimension, so it is singular

items.explain: Projections from 3D to 2D are modeled by singular matrices because they collapse a dimension, and a projection cannot be inverted.

items.prompt: In a regression, one input column is always exactly a multiple of another input column. What goes wrong with the normal equations matrix?

options.label: It becomes singular
It becomes the identity
It becomes triangular
It becomes smaller by one row

items.explain: Linearly dependent or collinear features make that matrix singular.

items.prompt: A regression has two features that always move together. What is often the fix?

options.label: Collect the same feature a third time
Multiply every entry by a large number
Drop or combine features, or use the pseudoinverse
Replace the data with all zeros

items.explain: The remedy is often to drop or combine features, or to use the pseudoinverse.

items.prompt: One column of a square matrix is exactly twice another column. What must be true of the map the matrix describes?

options.label: It is one-to-one and reversible
It maps every vector to zero
It doubles every vector
It is not one-to-one, so the matrix is singular

items.explain: A matrix is singular exactly when its columns are linearly dependent, and then the map is not one-to-one.

items.prompt: You solve a system of equations by Gaussian elimination, but the coefficient matrix is singular. What often happens?

options.label: A zero pivot appears that row swaps cannot fix
Every pivot is nonzero and a single answer appears
Row swaps always repair the zero pivot
The answer is always exactly zero

items.explain: With a singular matrix some pivots can be zero in a way row swaps cannot fix, and the result is often infinitely many solutions.
